The experiments show our contributions in the following aspects. First, we distinguish two types of model parameters,КТУ, and КРКО, for a taxonomy-order oilfield development task. Modeling КÐ may not improve model generalization because there exists a higher degree of feature correlation. To this,КТУ, there are two direct correlation structures directly embedded in our model, including topology structure and semantics structure. They should co-exist in the model structure. The topology structure evaluation is performed on the entire multi-element type-variable transaction dataset, i.e. \(D_{\mathrm{transaction\_cover}}^{P}\) which has \(44{,}955{,}347\) relevant elements. The semantics structure evaluation on multiple LexCon dataset involves \(9{,}915{,}288\) propositions. In this experiment, we find that the RO-POP score of the correlation structure \(K_{1}\) is the best among all the candidates. Second, for localization-specific information, neural network implementation is involved to model the granularity, which can improve the overall detection performance. For the experiment, we analyze the scoring performance on the Caltech dataset. For the type-subset prediction task, we evaluated the probability distribution of the entire sub-elements via dependency relations. Besides, it is good to score the text structure similarity between two utterances as higher ML probabilities show the more similar last utterance to the present one. This setting evaluates the whole utterance functionally without considering the latter. For the tag, Bidirectional LSTM can also obtain a better embedding than the single-directional LSTM.

Finally, we illustrate the other platform, KERNET, on the Caltech dataset. The detailed experimental results can be found in Table II. In this experiment, we see that despite the relatively high score, CTRD achieved the best performance but with high computation time.

In order to compare our models to the state-of-the-art models, we carried out the six evaluation benchmarks on the Caltech and Reuters datasets. As we see in Table III, CTRD achieves the best performance on the Reuters dataset. For the Caltech dataset, the CTRL-D dataset represent the overall state. Accordingly, it further draws the generalization or pre-training stage of COSINERK, which did not model post-transformation modules and could not do well on other implementations such as learning from scratch and knowledge distillation. From the overall score distribution on the Caltech dataset, Table IV, we can see that CTRD outperformed its competitors in almost all metrics by a large margin. However, for the other metrics, CTRD still gives about the best score. In summary, we comprehensively analyze the above experimental results and show that SOTONER-KERGET can indeed enhance the general ability of extraction and synonymous enhancement of distinct natural languages, shown by the more compact score distribution consistent with semantic granularities. It is worth reporting that though other models exceed CTRD with high accuracy on the knowledge distillation and foundation model stage, they usually have higher time cost. On the other hand, we conclude SOTONER-KERGET is a more effective manner for textual extraction and the synchronous optimization with VR 2 translates the shared similarity measure to diverse similarity measure. Besides, FLORUR can be more suitable for deep migration than COSINERK, due to its adaptive learning ability and fast convergence speed.

by IS highly depends on the choice of \(q(\mathbf{x})\). Equivalently, the sampling of \(X\) resolves the accuracy of approximation to \(\mathbb{E}_{p}[\mathbf{f}(X)]\).

The recipe of IS is to concentrate on the regions where the value is large, and avoid taking samples in regions where the value of the function is negligible [65]. It means that the amount of samples of a region should be proportional to the value the region has. If we think that a sample represents its neighbour region, then big value region means a big valued weight for its represented samples. We may get some intuition from the following simple example. Let \(X\) be a random variable and its density distribution be the triangular function \(f(x)=0.5(x-a)\) with \(x\in[a,a+2]\) for some positive number \(a\), which could be plotted like the left graph of Fig. 2. Accordingly, its cumulative distribution is \(F(x)=0.25(x-a)^{2}\) on the right of Fig. 2. Now we would think \(F(x)\) as \(q(\mathbf{x})\) (but not exactly). Then an IS could carry out as follows:

1. (a) Generate random numbers \(\zeta_{i}\in[0,1]\), \(i=1,2,\cdots,N.\)

2. (b) Then set \(F(x_{i})=\zeta_{i}\), and solve the \(x_{i}=F^{-1}(\zeta_{i})\),

where the \(F^{-1}\) stands for the inverse function of \(F\). As \(F(x)\) is a cumulative distribution function, the intervals with the same \(F\)-difference between its end points have the equal importance. So all the samples from such intervals have the equal importance. That is, a uniform \(F\)-value distribution would give an importance sampling. For example, in Fig. 2, the values \(\zeta=\{0,0.25,0.5,0.75,1\}\) give an importance sampling \(F^{-1}(\zeta)\)'s associated with weights \(\omega_{i}\) as follows.

\[\begin{array}[]{lllll}X_{1}&=F^{-1}(0)&=&a,&&\omega_{1}&=&0\\ X_{2}&=&F^{-1}(\frac{1}{4})&=&a+1,&&\omega_{2}&=&\frac{1}{\sqrt{2+\sqrt{3}}+3}\\ X_{3}&=&F^{-1}(\frac{1}{2})&=&a+\sqrt{2},&&\omega_{3}&=&\frac{\sqrt{2} }{\sqrt{2}+\sqrt{3}+3}\\ X_{4}&=&F^{-1}(\frac{3}{4})&=&a+\sqrt{3},&&\omega_{4}&=&\frac{\sqrt{3}}{ \sqrt{2+\sqrt{3}+3}}\\ X_{5}&=&F^{-1}(1)&=&a+2,&&\omega_{5}&=&\frac{\sqrt{2}}{2+\sqrt{3}+3}\end{array}\] (18)

These sample points are labeled by red crosses on \(x\)-coordinate in Fig. 2. It is clear that the number of sample points in each interval is proportional to the \(f\)-value at the center of that interval.

III. UNIFORMLY GEOMETRIC UNSCENTED FILTER

Each of the US, CS and IS is some kind of approximation for \(\int_{\mathbb{R}^{n}}\mathbf{f}(x)p(x)dx\) with different accuracy, efficiency and reliability. The US and CS are of good efficiency, but short on accuracy or reliability in case of acute nonlinearity and high dimensions. The IS showed good accuracy, but its high computational complexity hampers the application for higher dimensions. Summarily, the common challenge of all these methods is how to develop them for high dimensions. This section presents a scalable sampling scheme to tackle the challenge.

The basic idea of our novel sampling strategy is to reduce higher dimensional sampling to one dimensional case through an importance function (IF). The IF indicates the value of points. Then we make judicious choice of samples according to IF. Given a random variable \(X\), it is widely accepted that the mean \(\bar{\mathbf{x}}\) and covariance \(cov(\mathbf{x})\) has the highest importance. Indeed, in most cases, if these two and distribution are known then the density function \(p(\mathbf{x})\) could be completely formulated. In fact, US and CS make full use of this feature in their sampling. In this line of thinking, we say a positive value function \(i:\mathbb{R}^{n}\mapsto\mathbb{R}^{+}\) an importance function for an \(n\)-dimension random variable with mean \(\bar{\mathbf{x}}\), density distribution \(p(\mathbf{x})\) and probability distribution \(P(X)\), if it satisfies

1. (1) \(i(\bar{\mathbf{x}})\geq i(\mathbf{x})>0\), for all \(\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{n},\)

2. (2) \(i\) is upper semi-continuous,

3. (3) \(S_{\geq}(d):=\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\mid i(\mathbf{x})\geq d\}\) is compact and connected for any \(d\in\mathbb{R}^{+}\) with \(d>i_{0},\)

4. (4) for \(d\in\mathbb{R}^{+}\), \(p(\mathbf{x})=p(\mathbf{y})\) for any \(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{y}\in S_{=}(d)\), where \(S_{=}(d):=\{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\mid i(\mathbf{x})=d\},\)

5. (5) \(Y\) is a uniform distribution,

where \(i_{0}=\inf_{\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}}i(\mathbf{x})\) and \(Y\) is the distribution on \([i_{0},i(\bar{\mathbf{x}})]\) derived from probability distribution \(P(X\in S_{\geq}(d))\) for \(d\in[i_{0},i(\bar{\mathbf{x}})].\) Term 1) emphasizes the super importance of mean value. The continuity in 2) is a smoothing requirement for the IF. For a finite approximation, it imposes the compactness in 3). The condition 4) depicts an equal density distribution for equal importance points. A uniform distribution of \(d\) in 5) restricts the concentration on the IF such that we can unbiassly consider all importance references from IF. Note that the IF is not necessarily injective, i.e., \(|S_{=}(d)|\neq 1\), where \(|S|\) denotes the amount of elements in \(S.\) This means an equal importance of the different points in \(S_{=}(d).\) On the other side, \(S_{=}(d)\) and \(S_{\geq}(d)\) roughly specify certain region value specified by

i \(X(2)-i_{2}-i(i_{2})\)=\(c_{i}(d_{2}-d_{1},\)\(D=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{n}\mid d_{1}\leq i(x)\leq d_{2}\}\)(19)

Note that, the function \(i_{R}(\cdot)\) is a partial function over its domain \(\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^{n}),\) where \(\mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}^{n})\) is the power set of \(\mathbb{R}^{n}.\)

So the IF is critical to our sampling. In what follows, we discuss an IF based on the mean value, covariance matrix and probability distribution.

R_C(r) = \int_{x \in D_r} p(x) dx \tag{23}
\]

where \(\mathbb{R}^+\) is the set of nonnegative numbers. It is obvious that L(x) = 0 and \(R_C(0) = 1\).

Now we define an importance function \(i: \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}^+\) as

\[
i(x) = R_C(L(x)) \tag{24}
\]

\[
i(x) = \frac{1}{(2\pi)^{n/2}} \int_{y: y^T y \geq L(x)} \exp(-\frac{1}{2} y^T y) dy \tag{25}
\]

First, i(x) > 0, and i(x) = 1 ≥ i(x) for all x ∈ ℝⁿ. It is evident that i(·) is upper semi-continuous by the continuity of \(R_C(·)\) and \(L(·)\). From (23), \(i_0 = 0\), together with (24), it follows for any d > \(i_0\)
\[
S_{\succeq}(d) = \{x | i(x) \geq d\} = \{x | L(x) \leq r_d\} \tag{26}
\]

where r_d is the real number such that \(R_C(r_d) = d\). So \(S_{\succeq}(d)\) is compact and connected for all d > \(i_0\). Furthermore, it is not hard to show any x, y ∈ S_{\succeq}(d) implies \(p(x) = p(y)\) herein. Let \(L_d(r) := \{x | L(x) = r\}\) for the real numbers r > L(x), then it is actually S_d(d) = L_d(r_d) for any d > \(i_0\). At last, for the derived distribution Y from P(X ∈ S_{\succeq}(d)), we have
\[
P(Y \geq d) = P(X \in S_{\succeq}(d)) = P(D_{r_d}) = R_C(r_d) = d \tag{27}
\]

for d ∈ [0, 1] and so it has a uniform distribution. Therefore, the function i(·) defined by (24) is an IF. This IF is induced by the probability distribution function, which mainly concentrates on the characters of the probability distribution. In subsequent research, we are going to further investigate the construction of IF that is related to the integrand f(·) in \(\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} f(x) p(x) dx\). Moreover, it might be useful to study the IF that considers the characters of both integrands p(·) and f(·).

B. Uniformly Geometric Unscented Sampling

Based on previous importance function i(x), our sampling strategy runs as follows:

a) First, it generates uniformly distributed random numbers \(d_k \in [i_0, i(x)]\) with k = 1, 2, ..., \(N\) for some integer N.

b) Then we pick basic samples \(\mathcal{X}^*_{k_j}\) such that i(\(\mathcal{X}^*_{k_j}\)) = d_k, with \(1 \leq j \leq N_k\), for some integer N_k. For fixed k, all \(\mathcal{X}^*_{k,j}\)'s share the same importance value \(d_k\) and so should have the same weight \(\omega_{k,j}^*\).

ii) At last, we normalize the weights \(\omega_{k,j}^*\) and match the moments of x through adjusting the basic samples to obtain the final samples. Eventually, they jointly make a density approximation to the random variable X.

First of all, S = (d_k) & are disjoint for any sequence d_1 < ... < d_N and divide the spaces ℝⁿ into at most 2N + 1 many disjoint connected parts. It is natural to select the points from S = (d_k) to represent the region R_k := S \{(d_k) ∩ S_{d-(k-1)} for 1 < k ≤ N and R_1 := ℝⁿ - S \{(d_1) for k = 1, and there still three challenges to carry out the sampling scheme.

CH2 How to choose basic samples \(\mathcal{X}^*_{k,j}\) from the set S = ((d_k)?

CH3 What should be the proper weight distribution \(\omega_{k,j}^*\)?

For CH1, we employ the idea of IS to decide the amount of samples associated with d_k in what follows. As the points from S = ((d_k) could represent the region R_k, the importance value of R_k may be chosen as i_R(R_k) := d_k - d_{k-1}, the amount of samples from S = ((d_k) should be proportional to i_R(R_k). When the density function p(x) is known, we consider an alternative option that takes the samples {\(\mathcal{X}_{k,j}\)} with N_k proportional to the density function value p(\(\mathcal{X}_{k,j}\)), since the density value reflects certain importance of samples with respect to their surrounding regions. In PF, the samples are randomly picked from R_k of size proportional to i_R(R_k).

For CH2, we extend the idea of cubature rule by sampling symmetrically and evenly distributed in the set S = ((d_k), since all points in S = (d_k) have the same importance value. This can be achieved because of the symmetry of S = ((d_k) to the mean. Moreover, the samples here require more symmetry on the generators than CKF does, but it does not globally require the equal weights. To this end, we come up with a notion of uniformly geometric distribution (UGD). First we consider the UGD on the sphere U_n := {x ∈ ℝⁿ | x^T x = 1}. A finite sample set S ⊂ U_n is called a UGD if it satisfies the following conditions:
  
i) Each x ∈ S implies τ(x) ∈ S, where τ is an operation on coordinates of x which implements the permutation and/or sign changes of the coordinates.

ii) There is a constant d* such that for all x ∈ S, inf_{y ∈ S ||x - y|| = d*, where ||·|| is the Euclidean norm. The UGD, especially term b), presents a globally even spatial distribution of samples. In the next section, under the Gaussian density assumption, we will elaborate how to apply the spheres’ UGD to general sets like S = (d_k) which are not necessarily U_n anymore.

For CH3, it is natural to take \(\omega_{k,j}^*\) = p(\(\mathcal{X}^*_{k,j}\)) if the density distribution p(x) of x is known. This paper follows such rule under the density distribution assumption. When the density distribution p(x) is unknown, we suggest to consider the importance value i(\(\mathcal{X}^*_{k,j}\)) as the basic weight \(\omega_{k,j}^*\) of sample \(\mathcal{X}^*_{k,j}\). Similar to UKF, through moments matching, we compute the normalized weights and adjust the samples \(\mathcal{X}_{k,j}^*\) to approximate the density distribution of random variable X. IV. **Uniformly Geometric Distribution**

The previous section gave a framework of GUS and left the discussion about UGD to this section. We present here a detailed GUS of Gaussian random variables called geometric unscented *Gaussian sampling* (GMCGS).

We utilize the IF defined by (24) since the density function is known here. In this case, the importance values are in the interval \([0, 1]\). As a special case of the GUS method, the GMCGS first generates a uniformly distributed random numbers \(d_k \in [0, 1]\) ordered by increasing \(k\), where \(1 \leq k \leq N\) for some integer \(N\).

Normalization of Weights and Moments MatchingAs the density function \(p(\mathbf{x})\) is known, the basic weight \(\omega_{kj}^{*}\) of sample \(\mathcal{X}_{kj}^{*}\) of form (36) is \(\lambda\exp(-\frac{r_{k}}{2})\) computed by (20). However, the sampling \((\mathcal{X}_{kj}^{*},\omega_{kj})\) itself is not a proper approximation to \(X\), since it has a different covariance from \(X\). Even worse, the summation of \(\omega_{kj}^{*}\) is not unit in general.

A reasonable sampling with weighted samples should capture the statistics of a random variable. For a Gaussian random, the first two moments present all information. It is natural to consider the covariance matching. To this end, we adjust the samples \(\mathcal{X}_{kj}^{*}\) by some uniform stretch on them as follows

\[\mathcal{X}_{kj} = \overline{\mathbf{x}} + \sqrt{r_{k} + {\beta}}\sqrt{\mathbf{P}_X \mathcal{S}_j}, \mathcal{S}_j \in S_k \quad (37)\]

where \(S_k \subset U_n\) are UGD samplings set such that

\[|S_1| : |S_2| : ... : |S_N| \propto N_1 : N_2 : ... : N_N \quad (38)\]

Accordingly, we compute the samples' weighting values by

\[p(\mathcal{X}_{kj}) = \lambda \exp(-\frac{1}{2}(\mathcal{X}_{kj} - \overline{\mathbf{x}})\overline{\mathbf{P}^{-1}_x(\mathcal{X}_{kj} - \overline{\mathbf{x}}}^T ) \quad (39)\]

And then we normalize these weights by

\[\omega_{kj} = \frac{p(\mathcal{X}_{kj})}{\sum_{k \leq n}\omega_{kj} p(\mathcal{X}_{kj})} = \frac{\exp\{-\frac{1}{2} r_k\}}{\sum_{k \leq n} \exp\{-\frac{1}{2} r_k\} \sum_{j \leq n} j} \quad (40)\]

Here, the formula confirms that for a fixed \(k\), all samples \(\mathcal{X}_{kj}\) for different \(j\) have the same weight. Let \(w_k\) denote the same value of all \(\omega_{kj}\) for a fixed \(k\). By matching the mean and covariance, we have the following equations

\[\overline{\mathbf{x}} = \sum_{k \leq N} \sum_{j \leq n} \omega_{kj} \mathcal{X}_{kj}\] \[\mathbf{x} = \sum_{k \leq N} \sum_{j \leq n} \omega_{kj} \overline{\mathcal{X}}\] \[\mathbf{P}_x = \sum_{k \leq N} \sum_{j \leq n} \omega_{kj} (\mathcal{X}_{kj} - \overline{\mathbf{x}})(\mathcal{X}_{kj} - \overline{\mathbf{x}})^T.\]

\[\mathcal{X} = \sum_{k \leq N} \sum_{j \leq n} \omega_{kj} \mathcal{P}_X \mathcal{M}_k \mathcal{P}_X \mathcal{P}_X \quad (42)\]

.Moreover, the coeffcients in each term of the expansion converge to specific fixed points as \(n\) increases, as we discuss in the subsequent section.

Furthermore, the convergence of the series of expansion coefficients \(b_{n}^{*}(z)\) follows a similar logic. Let \(b_{n}^{*}(z)\) be the nth coefficient of the expansion of the function \(z\mapsto\Upsilon(z+\varepsilon)\) for any \(\varepsilon\ll 1\), where \(\Psi(n+\varepsilon):=\Psi(n+\tau({a}x))\) for any \(\tau({a})>0\). It is easy to show that we have \(b_{2k}^{*}(z)\approx 0\) for any \(z>\max\,({a}x)\,/\sqrt{M}\) and \(M=\bigl{(}\max\,({a}x)\,/\Psi(aa)\bigr{)}^{2}\). Indeed, \(n_{M}^{-1}\log p(n)^{-1}\) for \(n\geq M\) is bounded, and the exponential term is recorded in \(\Delta(n)\). Consequently,

\[b_{2k}^{*}(z)\approx\Bigl{\{}\begin{aligned} & n+\tau({a}x)(\log n)^{-1},&\text{if }z\gg 1\\ & 0,&\text{if }z\leqslant 1\end{aligned}\] (61)

The path-weighted expansion coefficients \(\Psi^{*}(n+\varepsilon)\) indeed converge at exponential rates to the corresponding path-weighted coefficients as \(n\to\infty\) - see Appendix B for detailed proof. We compare the results of neural expansion with the valid- or equivariant expansions from [see example 12 in], and show that the former consistently captures more complicated patterns (e.g., sequences like based on Augmented Lagrangian methods) and can be trained much faster (ability to evaluate closer to the stopping point). More generally, equivariant expansions learn a set of matrix linear functions while neural expansions learn a function representing the entrance to these \(M\) rows. The equivariant separation criterion (30) is indeed a second-order Taylor approximation for (28): \(\nabla y_{T}\neq 0\) rounds off to the second-order Taylor with the starting point \(\hat{y}_{T-1}\).

## 9 Numerical experiments

### Asymptopia

We motivate this application by asking how these properties generalize to case of mass-ratio optimization. We take a set of users in similar roles within the LUF network. Without any prior knowledge about the roles, we use the regularizations \(b(\mathbf{x})\) in (3) and suppress soft-thresholding.

Compared with a standard one-constraint quadratic problem, one additional constraint of the form

\[A(\mathbf{x})-\mu=\sqrt{(y_{0}-\hat{y})^{2}}\]

is added to the optimization problem (3). This version of the problem has no significance for extension of the Causal Formulation [21]. The gradient steps of \(\mathbf{u}_{k}\) (for \(f^{\lambda}_{k}\) in (2)) are described in a similar way, so the problem is essentially the same as promoting student (or group of students) interests over time, performing a task. While in the regularized one-constraint problem, estimation returns \(\mathbf{A}^{\operatorname{E}}(\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{E})\), the gradient step uses attractive gradients instead of \(\hat{\mathbf{A}}_{0}\), corresponding to \(\mathbf{y}=\nu\Lambda^{\operatorname{E}}(\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{E})\), in which case one could expect its gradient to decay like \(\bigl{/}\bigl{|}\nu\Lambda^{\operatorname{E}}(\hat{\mathbf{A}}^{E})\bigr{|}^{2}\) along many small subspaces, much like gradient methods applied to homogeneous descent in \(\log p(a/x)\) are done in the dual problem, which is the usual conditional log-likelihood of saw-toothed anarchy [21].

### Nonconcavity

The observation \(b_{k}^{2}(z)=1\) implies nonconcavity of the Lagrangian for \(r>t\): \(\chi_{k}+A^{\lambda}_{k}\geq\chi_{k+t}+A^{\lambda}_{k+t}\). Regularization policies add some concave \(\Omega\) to \(B\); variants with imposed adaptation level (stringency) [see (21)] could simply be seen as a convexification. This property can also carry over exponentially to \(\psi(z)\): if \(r/t\log r\) is relatively small, the Lagrangian is more like \(\psi(z)\frac{e^{B\mu}-\exp(B)}{B\mu}\) (up to small multiplicative constant \(C>0\) that has to be found)
